newsitem.title: TURKEY: Early polls may batter Turkish economy, markets.
newsitem.headline: Early polls may batter Turkish economy, markets.

text.p: Turkey's inflation-ridden economy and its financial markets may face hard times if negotiations between Turkish coalition partners produce early elections, analysts said on Friday.

Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan was due to meet Tansu Ciller, leader of the coalition's junior partner True Path Party (DYP), on Friday to bargain over possible early elections to solve a government crisis over Islamist activism.
Economists fear the government will increase public spending ahead of elections and ignore monetary discipline.

Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller gave the first suggestion of such a move on Thursday when she announced higher-than-expected grain purchase prices -- seen by analysts as a move to win support from millions of farmers.
Government officials say the state-run Grain Board (TMO) will need financial backing from the central bank and the tresury to finance the purchases, which might distort monetary policy.
The central bank has not extended a loan to the TMO since 1994 as part of its tight monetary policy, which bankers say has kept Turkey out of financial crisis despite frequent political turmoil.

Easier monetary policy and increased spending and lira liquidity ahead of an early election would probably boost demand for the dollar, put the national currency under pressure, fuel inflation, running at around 77 percent a year, and widen the budget deficit.
Interest rates may also climb because the cash-short treasury would be likely to borrow more from domestic markets to finance pre-election spending.
On Friday bond yields rose by one point to 102.5 percent and the lira weakened to 140,420 versus the dollar from Thursday's close of 140,300 on political uncertainty.
Financial stability, secured by central bank control and tight monetary policies, may also be put at risk if the treasury fails to borrow and leaves the excess money in the market.

Bankers say the treasury is expected to give a signal about its future attitude next week when it will probably set a domestic borrowing auction to finance its bond redemption of 289 trillion lira ($2 billion) on Wednesday.
The market expects the treasury to set the auction at maturity of less than one-year.
Bankers say the treasury may not gather enough demand from banks, scared by the political crisis, if it insists on holding a long-term bond auction.

The treasury has successfuly extended the average domestic borrowing maturity to over one year from around three months and officials say cabinet ministers are inclined to reject any maturity to lower the average.
Efforts to draw up a medium-term anti-inflationary programme might also be shelved if the decision for early elections is taken by parliament.

The Istanbul stock exchange index, which dived 2.3 percent on Thursday on fears of snap elections, rose 1.1 percent in the morning session on Friday on expectations that the government would collapse and there would be talks on forming a new coalition rather than holding fresh elections.

The main opposition Motherland Party is planning to file a new censure motion to topple Erbakan's Islamist-led government next week as four more MPs are expected to resign from the junior coalition partner DYP on Monday.
Former health minister Yildirim Aktuna announced his resignation from the DYP on Friday, robbing the coalition of its absolute majority in parliament.
The coalition partners are planning to win support from a seven-MP far-right party to maintain an effective parliament majority.
